messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Minh's Story

Minh was twenty-four when his boyfriend Marcus hit him for the first time. It was a Thursday evening in their shared apartment in Portland, and Minh had mentioned—almost casually—that he'd run into an old friend at the grocery store. Marcus's face darkened. He accused Minh of flirting, of betraying him, of being exactly the kind of person who couldn't be trusted. When Minh tried to explain, Marcus shoved him hard against the kitchen counter. The impact came suddenly; Minh's head struck the edge, and for a moment the room tilted. He remembered the shock more than the pain at first—the sense that the person he loved had become someone else entirely, someone whose hands were weapons. What came next blurred: Marcus screaming, Minh's own voice small and apologetic, the physical force of being pushed down, the feeling of his body going rigid, shutting down, unable to move or fight back. Some moments remained vivid—the exact angle of light through the kitchen window, the smell of Marcus's cologne mixed with rage—while others had dissolved into fog. Minh couldn't quite reconstruct the sequence of what happened after he fell, only fragments that refused to arrange themselves into a coherent story.

The relationship continued for another eight months. There were apologies, flowers, promises. There were also more incidents, each one preceded by Minh's increasing certainty that he had done something wrong, that he was the kind of person who provoked this, who deserved it. By the time he finally left, Minh had come to believe that the violence was somehow intrinsic to who he was—that his inadequacy, his neediness, his very existence in spaces where he didn't belong had drawn this out of Marcus. He carried that belief like a stone in his chest.

Now, three months into his escape, Minh works as a painter for a commercial contractor. The job itself is stable, but his mind is not. Unwanted thoughts about the abuse surface without warning—fragments of Marcus's voice, the sensation of being pinned, the taste of his own blood. These intrusions arrive most often in the late afternoon, that particular hour when the light changes and the apartment grows quiet, and Minh has learned to dread it. He has stopped painting in the evenings. He avoids the times of day when his mind seems most vulnerable to these memories, staying at the job site longer, finding reasons to be elsewhere, anything to postpone the moment he must be alone with his thoughts. The uncertainty gnaws at him too—a constant low-level dread that something bad is about to happen, that he's missing some crucial sign of danger. When his current supervisor mentions that a project might take longer than scheduled, Minh's chest tightens immediately. His mind jumps to catastrophe: something is wrong, someone is coming, he has failed in some invisible way.

These fears drive his scanning. The moment Minh enters any room—his apartment, the job site office, a coffee shop—his eyes move automatically to the exits. He counts them. He notes which ones are blocked, which might be too slow. He listens constantly for sounds that shouldn't be there: a key in the lock, footsteps on the stairs, a car door slamming outside. His body remains in a state of low-grade vigilance, always listening, always watching for the moment when the threat will materialize. At work, when a colleague approaches from behind, Minh freezes completely. His body locks up, his breath catches, and for a few seconds he is unable to move or speak. It is as though the memory itself is happening in real time—he is back on the kitchen floor, paralyzed, waiting for the next blow.

The more Minh scans for danger, the more his mind produces it. He begins to avoid anything that reminds him of Marcus: certain songs, certain neighborhoods, even the smell of a particular cologne brand triggers a cascade of intrusive memories and the conviction that he is being watched, that Marcus has found him, that this is somehow his fault for being the kind of person Marcus wanted to hurt. His avoidance of these cues only strengthens them. The more he runs from reminders, the more his mind treats them as genuine threats. Each time he freezes when startled, each time he scans a room for exits, each time he lies awake listening for sounds in the dark, he reinforces the idea that danger is real and imminent. And each time he experiences that imminent danger, the memories surface again—vivid, disjointed, feeling as though they are occurring in the present moment rather than the past. The fragmented quality of the memories, the moments that are crystal clear alongside the blank spaces, makes it impossible for him to feel that the trauma is truly over. His mind cannot construct a coherent narrative of what happened, and so it keeps trying, keeps looping back, keeps producing new versions of the threat.

The belief that he belongs nowhere has become self-fulfilling. Minh has pulled away from his family, from the few friends who remained after the relationship consumed so much of his life. He tells himself they would judge him if they knew—that he should have seen the signs, should have been stronger, should have been different. When his mother calls, he lets it go to voicemail. When his coworkers invite him out after a shift, he declines, certain that he would only bring them down, that his presence would somehow contaminate the evening. The isolation deepens his sense that he is fundamentally inadequate, that something about his character made him vulnerable to abuse. This belief, in turn, makes him hypervigilant about any sign that others are watching him, judging him, preparing to reject him or harm him. He scans their faces for disapproval the way he scans rooms for exits.

Minh came to his first therapy appointment last week, referred by his primary care physician who had noticed his weight loss and the dark circles under his eyes. He sat in the waiting room for ten minutes before entering, noting the exits, counting the people in the space, measuring the distance to the door. What he wants most is to stop being afraid. What he fears most is that the fear is justified—that he really is the broken, inadequate person he believes himself to be, and that no amount of therapy will change that fundamental truth.
